# Current

[Scroll Down](https://www.duanethomasgallery.com/blog/home/current/#post-inner)

Women’s Drawings, Feminist Works on Paper

Opening October 2, 2026 with a reception 6/8 pm 
Duane Thomas Gallery, New York

137 West Broadway, 3rd floor

NY, NY 10013

Women’s Drawings, Feminist Works on Paper examines the importance of paper as a medium for women artists working during the emergence of feminist art in the 1960s and 1970s, while tracing the persistence of these concerns into the present. Rather than treating drawing as secondary to painting, sculpture, or performance, the exhibition considers the sheet of paper as an intimate and adaptable site of artistic inquiry—one capable of holding the personal, the political, the domestic, the experimental, and the documentary. The exhibition brings together artists whose approaches to paper range from the direct observation of the body to journals and notebooks, pattern, domestic materials, historical research, and the recording of women’s lives.

This history is closely connected to the pioneering work of critic and curator Lucy R. Lippard, whose 1971 exhibition Twenty Six Contemporary Women Artists at the Aldrich Museum of Contemporary Art brought together a generation of women artists working across a remarkably diverse range of practices. Among them were Cynthia Carlson, Shirley Pettibone, and Barbara Zucker all represented here.

It is within this expanded field that the exhibition turns specifically to paper. A substantial group of drawings by Eunice Golden, made between 1963 and 1970, offers an intimate entry into the artist’s early investigation of the body, sexuality, and representation. Working on paper allowed Golden to approach these subjects with immediacy and freedom, and her drawings reveal a sustained engagement with the figure at a moment when women artists were increasingly questioning who had the authority to represent the body. Presented together, the drawings are not studies for another medium but a substantial body of work in their own right, demonstrating the capacity of drawing to become a direct and personal means of confronting sexuality and the female experience.

Cynthia Carlson’s drawings similarly make the materiality of paper central to the work. Safety pins and other metal sewing pins are attached directly to the sheets, puncturing and organizing the surface. Materials associated with sewing and domestic labor are transformed into elements of drawing, collapsing the distinction between traditionally feminine craft and contemporary art. Carlson’s notebooks extend this practice into a more intimate form of recording and research. They are presented alongside the journals of Shirley Pettibone, whose drawings and notebooks from the mid-1960s demonstrate how writing and image can coexist within the same artistic space. In both artists’ work, the notebook becomes a place for thinking through drawing—a form that can remain provisional, accumulative, private, and unfinished.

Joyce Kozloff’s Tepotzlan (1973) introduces another important dimension. Characteristic of Kozloff’s engagement with pattern and decoration, the work reflects the expanded interest of the 1970s in ornament, repetition, craft, and decorative structures. Pattern offered artists a means of questioning the hierarchies that had historically separated the supposedly serious from the supposedly decorative, and fine art from forms of production traditionally associated with women.

Barbara Zucker’s works concerning wet nursing extend the role of paper into historical and social research. The exhibition includes an installation of works made during the 1990s, resulting from Zucker’s sustained investigation of wet nursing and its histories. Here drawing becomes a form of inquiry: paper serves as a place where historical information, bodily experience, research, and memory can accumulate. The work brings into view a largely overlooked history of women’s labor and the ways in which women’s bodies have been understood, used, and regulated.

The exhibition’s concerns extend into the twenty-first century with Mimi Smith’s Timelines series (2007). Comprising two drawings of onesies—one associated with a baby and the other with a young girl—the works approach women’s lives with the humor and detached curiosity of an archaeologist reconstructing a civilization from its surviving objects. Smith’s deceptively simple garments become markers within a chronology: the objects of childhood are placed within a larger trajectory of female life, suggesting the successive stages through which the female body and its reproductive possibilities are culturally understood. With wit and economy, the works invite us to consider the breadth of women’s reproductive lives not as a single biological event but as a chronology extending from childhood through adulthood and beyond.

Smith’s Timelines also introduces a different conception of drawing into the exhibition. The garment is not represented for its own sake; it becomes evidence. Like an artifact recovered from another culture, the onesie can be read as a clue to the social expectations, identities, and conditions surrounding women’s lives. The humor of the work is therefore inseparable from its critical perspective. By imagining the history of women through objects and stages of dress, Smith transforms the familiar into something strange enough to be examined anew.

Taken together, these works propose a history of feminist drawing that is not defined by a particular image or style. Instead, it emerges through different relationships to materials and methods: the intimacy of the sheet, the immediacy of the hand, the notebook as a place of thought, sewing materials transformed into drawing, pattern reclaimed from the category of decoration, historical research carried through repeated acts of looking and recording, and the reconstruction of women’s lives through the objects that surround them.

Paper, in this context, is more than a support. It becomes a place where women’s experiences can be observed, documented, questioned, remembered, and reimagined. From Golden’s bodies of the 1960s to Smith’s archaeological humor of 2007, these artists demonstrate how drawing can make visible forms of experience that have often existed at the margins of art history. More than fifty years after Lippard’s Twenty Six Contemporary Women Artists, the exhibition continues that expanded understanding of what women’s art can be: not a singular style, but a multiplicity of ways of looking at women’s bodies, histories, labor, sexuality, domestic lives, and reproductive experience.

Pot Shop IV NY

Ed. Varie is pleased to present Pot Shop, a group exhibitions with opening reception Friday April 20, 7–10pm at Ed. Varie, 184 E. 7th Street, New York, NY. 

Pot Shop is a light hearted and loosely curated group show paying homage to everything POT(s) related in a variety of disciplines and styles. Fourth Annual Pot Shop returns to its roots in New York with work that celebrates vessels in all forms, medium and dimension; fine art, functional, and sculptural. 

Pot Shop includes multi-dimensional works by Alexandra Defoe, Amanda Valdez, Dean Roper, DK Somethings (Denise Kupferschmidt and TD Sidell's Object Shop), EVE (Ed. Varie Editions) Future Retrieval (collaborative works by Guy Michael Davis and Katie Parker), Guy Overfelt, Jessie Rose Vala, and Kyle Quinn. 

Gallery hours are 12-5pm Saturday and Sunday and also by appointment. Exhibition will run through May 13. For any additional information please contact the gallery director, info@edvarie.com. 

Amanda Valdez, Valley Vessel, 2017, Screenprint on yellow French's paper, 19 x 25 in. Edition of 35. 

Kyle Quinn, Burning Bush (Denver, 2016), Polaroid, Custom Frame, 8 x 6 inches. 

Future Retrieval & Amanda Valdez, Vessel Cult 39, 2018, Stoneware, 16 x 20 x 20 inches, Stoneware, drawing transfer and glaze. 

Future Retrieval, Sloyd, Cyprus, 2017, Wood, Dimensions vary.

_Samsøñ_ creates and presents programs that explore the diversity of cultures and voices that continually shape contemporary art and ideas today, introducing emerging and under-recognized artists as well as re-contextualizing established artists. It is our mission to act as an interdisciplinary laboratory for the convergence of film, video, performance, music, design and visual art.

There is no solution to the question or argument; not zero and not infinite. A condition: there is no question or argument that can support an answer. For every element of ∅ the property holds (vacuous truth); There is no element of ∅ for which the property holds.

_Samsøñ is a member of the_ [_New Art Dealers Alliance (NADA)_](http://www.newartdealers.org/)_._

Camilo Alvarez was born in 1976 in New York, NY, and resides in Boston, MA. He was born to Dominican parents and lived in Santo Domingo for 7 years. He received a B.A. in Art History from Skidmore College (Saratoga Springs, NY) and a Masters of Liberal Arts in Museum Studies from Harvard University (Cambridge, MA).

He has worked at Exit Art (NY, NY), Socrates Sculpture Park (Queens, NY), MIT’s List Visual Art Center (Cambridge, MA) and the Skowhegan School of Painting & Sculpture (NY, NY & Skowhegan, ME). He sits on the National Advisory Council for Skidmore College’s Tang Teaching Museum and the Advisory Board of for Tufts University Art Galleries. He also serves as Co-Chair of the Advisory Board at the Institute of Contemporary Art, Boston and is a Commissioner on the Boston Art Commission.

He is the Owner, Director and Preparator at Samsøñ, formerly Samson Projects, founded in 2004. He has given solo exhibitions to William Pope.L (2010), Rebecca Morris (2006), Kader Attia (2008), and Beverly Semmes (2017) among many. Samsøn’s programs and exhibitions have been reviewed by the New York Times, ArtForum, the Boston Globe and Flash Art. The gallery has participated in art fairs including VOLTA (Basel, Switzerland & NY, NY), ARCO (Madrid, Spain) MACO (Mexico City, Mexico), NADA (Miami, FL & NY, NY), MECA (San Juan, PR) and the Armory (NY, NY). Samsøñ placed works in the permanent collections of LACMA, the Tate, MWoods, MOMA, the Guggenheim, the Leslie Lohman Museum of Gay and Lesbian Art, the Perez Art Museum Miami, the Museum of Fine Arts Boston and the Institute of Contemporary, Boston among others. In 2010, Samsøñ commenced sübsamsøn, a form of artist’s residency.

The Landing is dedicated to establishing a dialogue between under-appreciated historical artists and contemporary practices.  The gallery will maintain a program of solo and two-person exhibitions, as well as thematic group exhibitions throughout the year at its Los Angeles location.

The Landing was founded in 2012 by Gerard O’Brien, owner of Reform Gallery on Melrose Avenue in Los Angeles.  In 2015, the Landing will open as its own gallery, a 2800-square-foot location on Jefferson Boulevard in Los Angeles.

Carol Szymanski: _You Pair How_

February 17 – March 26, 2022

Opening Reception: 
February 17, 2022 
6:00 - 8:00pm

[Carol Szymanski CV](https://www.signsandsymbols.art/artists/carol-szymanski)

**signs and symbols** is pleased to present _You Pair How_, a new exhibition by [**Carol Szymanski**](https://signsandsymbols.art/artists/carol-szymanski), which continues the artist’s ongoing investigation into the transmutability of language. Szymanski’s long-standing interest in translating language and speech visually — beginning with her first solo show _The Broken Phoneme_ in 1987, which broke down words to their basic and distinct parts, their phonemes — extends itself now to the analysis and translation of gesture, crediting it as the natural visual action of expression. _The Go-Between_, a match-making project in which Szymanski plays the artist-matchmaker to anonymous participants, gives her the material to isolate and watch gesture in action. The “go-arounds” (or dates), captured in video and transmuted into Polaroid photography, sound, and a wall painting incorporating neon, speak aesthetically to the underlying properties and patterns of gesture itself.

Speaking on phases of gesture, the prominent linguist Adam Kendon notes, “The preparation phase is the movement of the hand as it readies itself for the gestural stroke. The stroke phase is the most effortful and most meaningful phase of the gesture.” With this concept providing a formal backbone for the artist’s project, Szymanski works to segment hand gestures from the stream of gestural activity in the “go-arounds.” By slowing down, zooming in, cutting up, and overall abstracting the participants’ hand movements, gesture becomes disconnected from its corresponding words and phrases — becomes something existing in its own right, a visual language that, depending on the discussion or the person whose hand it is, can either be punchy, deliberate, or delicate. These works point to the idea that gesture, an accoutrement to words, goes beyond syllables and the phonemes, and is perhaps closer to the emotion and intensity of the original expression.

Adding to the power of the gestural expression is the fact that these images derive from people who have been “paired” by Szymanski, by way of a system involving interviews as well as a questionnaire (adapted from the nonsensical questionnaire in Hal Ashby's 1971 cult film _Harold and Maude_). The matchmaking performance, active for a year, is rooted in Szymanski’s love of bringing people together, but also in her ongoing attempt to question the boundaries between life and art, or better yet, to efface the boundaries of art so as to make it indistinguishable from life. As the artist phrases it: “You might think of the performance as a sort of social sculpture, or perhaps a collaging of people. The basis of trust stems from my good will, discerning eye, and innate desire to bring people together for the sake of happiness.” As of today, she has conducted 32 “go-arounds” where couples meet each other in her studio or sometimes on zoom. They play a few rounds of poker with her for warm-up and then Szymanski leaves them to have a date.

The performance is open to audience participation. If you or a friend would like to join the pool, please email thego-between@emergencyeyewash.org. 

**carol szymanski**'s art spans many media, from sculpture and painting to video and performance. She has become particularly known for a series of sculptures in the form of invented musical instruments, and particularly brass horns shaped from the alphabet, that she has been making since 1993. Szymanski was born in Charlotte, North Carolina, studied at the San Francisco Art Institute and the Whitney Museum Studio Program, and lives and works in New York. Recent solo and collaborative exhibitions include _He Said, I Thought_, signs and symbols, New York (2019); _Pareidolia_, Totah Gallery, New York (2018); _The Phonemophonic Alphabet Brass Band_, Winter Garden, New York (2017) curated by John Schaefer, WNYC New Sounds Live Series; _Emergency Eyewash_ with Barry Schwabsky, Tanja Grunert Gallery, New York (2017); _A Distance as Close as It Can Be,_ Elga Wimmer PCC, New York (2016); _My Life is an Index_, Tanja Grunert Gallery, New York (2015); and _Pissing Against the Wind, or, Sketches on the Mental Drain on the Dead Banker_, Guided by Invoices, New York (2012), which have received press attention in Artcritical, Art Press, Brooklyn Rail, Hyperallergic, and Time Out New York. She has been a recipient of numerous awards including the Rome Prize and a National Endowment for the Arts fellowship. Szymanski has also collaborated with numerous composers and musicians including Ben Neill, Ekmeles Ensemble, Betsy McClelland, Dewey Redman, and Wadada Leo Smith. Most recently, in the fall of 2021, Szymanski also presented the performance _Phonemophonic Alphabet Brass Band_ with avant-garde trumpeter, jaimie branch, at Park Avenue Armory.

# **Three-Legged Stool**

## **October 30–December 20**

**A collaboration with Holsum Gallery, Kansas City**

**Opening reception: Friday, Oct 30, 6 pm — 8 pm**

The art world that matters most is not a monolith but a vast, idiosyncratic network of makers and exhibition spaces, sustained largely by the particular energies of obsessed individuals with singular visions. Nowhere is this more evident than in the Midwest, where independent spirits and regional prerogatives thrive precisely because they do not answer to prevailing conventions. This autonomy keeps the work unique, but it also renders much of it invisible to broader cultural interests.

Occasionally, it is worth looking up from the local terrain and toward the horizon—to fold a few of these regional eddies into a shared current, if only temporarily. Collaboration and exchange can function as a way of redistributing energy, feeding it back into local systems rather than siphoning it away.

A three-legged stool is the minimum structure required for balance. It is stable, but only just—an apt metaphor for the desire to approach destabilization without collapsing into comfort or stasis. Three Legged Stool brings together three exhibition programs—Holsum Gallery (Kansas City), Project, Project (Omaha), and Real Tinsel (Milwaukee)—each of which embraces and amplifies the eccentricities of its local scene. The exhibition temporarily transports these distinct sensibilities into one another’s ecosystems, allowing local flavors to intermingle, seep, and subtly alter the conditions of their host environments. The goal is not synthesis or consensus, but exposure: to generate examples of exchange that are beneficial and enduring, even as each program ultimately returns to the business of being local weirdos, sustained by the particular nutrients of their own communities.

The soul of the art world lies in odd individuals operating with singular commitment. Still, from time to time, it’s worth adding a leg or two—even if it’s just to offer someone else a place to sit.

[**Art Basel Miami Beach — I Could See the Water at the Edge of All Things**](https://spinelloprojects.com/program/#art-basel-miami-beach-i-could-see-the-water-at-the-edge-of-all-things)

12\. 02 – 06\. 2026

_Bookending its 20th anniversary season, Spinello Projects makes its debut in the Galleries sector of Art Basel Miami Beach (Booth A5), marking a significant milestone for the gallery._

_I Could See the Water at the Edge of All Things_, a curated group show, brings together Miami-based artists Elliot & Erick Jiménez (b. 1989, Miami, FL), Marlon Portales (b. 1991, Pinar Del Rio, Cuba) , and Nina Surel (b. 1971, Buenos Aires, Argentina) in a multigenerational dialogue exploring the body as a site of memory, transformation, and spiritual encounter, where color becomes a language connecting the physical and metaphysical worlds.

Working across photography, painting, and sculpture, the artists draw from personal histories, ancestral traditions, and the layered identities of the Latin American and Caribbean diaspora. A shared chromatic language of deep, resonant blues unifies the presentation, evoking water, sky, spiritual depth, and the liminal spaces between the physical and metaphysical. Enveloped in blue, the booth becomes an immersive environment where individual practices converge.

Elliot & Erick Jiménez construct staged photographic compositions that draw from Cuba's layered cultural history, ancestral traditions, and personal experiences to create their own visual mythologies. Incorporating symbolic objects and ritual elements, their works explore the fluid boundaries between the earthly and otherworldly, where inherited histories are reimagined through personal narratives. Marlon Portales presents lush, psychological landscapes in which human figures merge with nature, blurring the distinction between interior and exterior worlds. His paintings contemplate desire, displacement, and belonging through environments that become extensions of the human psyche. Nina Surel's ceramic sculptures draw from feminine archetypes, mythology, and Florida's wetland ecology, merging human, botanical, and animal forms into hybrid figures. Through the tactile language of clay, her works explore the relationship between materiality, the natural world, and cycles of life and regeneration.

Together, the artists envision the body as both landscape and archive, a site where inherited histories, spiritual beliefs, and personal experiences intertwine. Through distinct yet interconnected visual languages, _I Could See the Water at the Edge of All Things_considers how these histories take shape, revealing the shifting relationships between the human, natural, and spiritual realms.

[**From His Rib**](https://spinelloprojects.com/program/#from-his-rib)

12\. 01 – 06\. 2026

Spinello Projects presents _From His Rib_, an exhibition bringing together Cuban-American artist Amy Bravo and identical twin artists Elliot & Erick Jiménez in a dialogue exploring the intersections of mythology, spirituality, gender, and inherited power. Working across painting, photography, sculpture, and assemblage, the artists draw from their shared Cuban heritage, queer identities, and personal histories to challenge and reimagine the religious and cultural narratives that shape identity and belonging.

Taking its title from Bravo's reinterpretation of the biblical creation of Eve, the exhibition examines the relationship between creation and autonomy, inheritance and transformation. In Bravo's work, a woman emerges from a horned figure, wielding one of its broken horns against its creator in an act of liberation. This symbolic reversal finds a striking parallel in the Jiménez brothers' Red Chapel, where the Afro-Cuban orisha Changó undergoes a transformation through Saint Barbara, his Catholic counterpart, reflecting the spiritual resilience and cultural survival embedded within Lucumí traditions. Across their respective practices, the artists reclaim symbols of patriarchal and spiritual authority, challenging fixed notions of gender, power, and identity.

Together, Bravo and Elliot & Erick Jiménez explore the contradictions of inheritance: the desire to preserve what has been passed down while resisting the structures that have historically constrained it. Through a queer reimagining of sacred narratives, familial mythology, and cultural memory, _From His Rib_ proposes identity not as something predetermined by origin, but as an ongoing process of reclamation, reinvention, and self-determination.

[**Becoming Landscape**](https://spinelloprojects.com/program/#becoming-landscape)

11\. 30 – 01\. 09. 2027

Spinello Projects presents _Becoming Landscape_, the second solo exhibition with the gallery by Cuban-American artist Marlon Portales, featuring new paintings that explore the intimate relationship between the human body and the natural world. Proposing that the body is itself a landscape, the exhibition considers identity as a state of perpetual metamorphosis, shaped by memory, migration, and the places we inhabit, leave behind, or reconstruct through imagination.

At the heart of the exhibition is the human figure, depicted in moments of contemplation, vulnerability, desire, and transcendence. Solitary and gathered bodies inhabit lush, dreamlike environments where the boundaries between figure and landscape begin to dissolve. Nature is neither passive nor merely a backdrop; it becomes an extension of the body, just as the body becomes an extension of the natural world. These encounters suggest a fluid relationship between the physical and spiritual, the internal and external.

Migration and displacement inform Portales’s exploration of belonging. His experience leaving Cuba has shaped his understanding of landscape, revealing how places persist within us even as they are altered by distance, time, and memory. Drawing from lived experiences, dreams, and imagined environments, his paintings evoke spaces that feel simultaneously familiar and impossible to locate. These psychological landscapes exist beyond fixed narratives, where memory and imagination converge.

An important conceptual touchstone is the work of Cuban-American artist Ana Mendieta, whose investigations into body, earth, memory, and belonging resonate throughout the exhibition. Particularly influential are the spiritual and ritual dimensions of her practice, in which the body merges with the landscape, simultaneously disappearing into the earth and leaving behind a trace of its presence. This relationship between presence and absence echoes Portales’s own inquiries into displacement and the ways the body preserves the memory of its origins.

Working in oil on canvas and wood panel, Portales draws upon the historical traditions of painting while cultivating a distinctly contemporary visual language. Expressive brushwork, luminous color, transparency, and the sensuality of paint animate his compositions, preserving the physical gestures of their making.

_Becoming Landscape_ dissolves the distinctions between portrait and landscape, body and nature, memory and dream. Rather than suggesting the disappearance of identity, this merging proposes an understanding of the self as fluid, evolving, and perpetually becoming. Landscape exists not only around us, but within us—in the memories we carry, the places we have left behind, and the possibilities of who we might yet become.

[**The Armory Show — Elliot & Erick Jiménez**](https://spinelloprojects.com/program/#the-armory-show-elliot-erick-jimenez)

09\. 24 – 27\. 2026

**Spinello Projects presents What We Are Becoming, a solo booth by Elliot & Erick Jiménez at The Armory Show.** 

Elliot & Erick Jiménez are identical twin artists whose practice draws from photography, mixed media, sculpture, and installation to construct immersive worlds that explore memory, migration, spirituality, and the fluid nature of identity. Rooted in their experience as first-generation Cuban Americans and informed by Afro-Caribbean cosmologies, their work brings together Lucumí traditions, Western iconography, and art historical references to create a dialogue where inherited histories and contemporary experience converge.

This new body of work marks the artists’ first major series following El Monte, their debut solo museum exhibition at the Pérez Art Museum Miami. Rather than departing from the questions that shaped that exhibition, these works represent a subtle evolution, one that shifts attention from the search for identity toward the continual process of transformation.

As first-generation Cuban Americans raised within an Afro-Cuban household, they have long grappled with the experience of belonging simultaneously to inherited and imagined homelands. While physically removed from the island, they continue to negotiate the traditions, stories, and spiritual lineages passed down. In this sense, these works inhabit an interior landscape—one that holds ancestry, memory, and identity in constant dialogue.

Across the series, the anonymous figures that have long occupied the Jiménez brothers’ visual language begin to undergo subtle yet profound changes. Shadow bodies dissolve into flowers, others emerge in luminous white, or exist suspended between fire, the natural world, and ritual. Rather than functioning as fixed symbols, these figures inhabit states of becoming, resisting singular definitions and stable identities. Their transformation mirrors the layered realities of Caribbean culture itself, where histories of migration, syncretism, adaptation, and survival have continually reshaped notions of self and belonging.

[**The Hero’s Journey**](https://spinelloprojects.com/program/#the-heros-journey)

09\. 12 – 10\. 31. 2026

Spinello presents Gabriel Pozzo’s debut solo exhibition with the gallery, _The Hero’s Journey._

In _The Hero’s Journey,_ Gabriel Pozzo chronicles a decade shaped by migration, self-discovery, and artistic transformation following his departure from Venezuela. Drawing from Joseph Campbell’s seminal work on comparative mythology, The Hero with a Thousand Faces, Pozzo considers the archetypal hero’s journey through the lens of the contemporary diasporic experience: departure becomes a threshold, displacement a landscape of uncertainty and adaptation, and the search for home inseparable from the search for self.

Drawing from the dreamlike logic of magical realism, Pozzo transforms the rituals of everyday life into psychologically charged scenes. The artist appears throughout the paintings as both protagonist and witness, inviting the viewer into intimate moments of commuting, working, showering, sleeping, and shared intimacy. Familiar spaces become subtly destabilized; reality bends just enough for memory, desire, solitude, and longing to surface beneath the ordinary.

Intimate fragments of the artist’s past and present are woven throughout the exhibition. Lingering memories of Venezuela coexist with experiences of family loss, displacement, and the embrace of Pozzo’s queer identity after leaving home. Rather than unfolding chronologically, these moments surface as recollections, dreams, and emotional impressions, collapsing the distance between the life that was left behind and the one constructed in its wake.

Across the exhibition, the joys and challenges of the past decade become markers of transformation—a period in which inherited and former identities are questioned, resilience is forged, and a more fully realized sense of self emerges. Migration is presented not simply as a departure from one place and arrival in another, but as an ongoing process of becoming. In _The Hero’s Journey_, home is ultimately both a place and something constructed within oneself.

[**NADA NY — Esaí Alfredo**](https://spinelloprojects.com/program/#nada-ny-esai-alfredo)

05\. 13 – 17\. 2026

**Spinello Projects presents** **_Te Llevo / I Carry You_****, a solo booth by Miami-based painter Esaí Alfredo (b. 1997, Puerto Rico) at NADA New York.** 

Expanding on his ongoing exploration of memory, belonging, and queer identity, Alfredo’s latest body of work unfolds as a sequence of intimate, narrative-driven paintings that trace the emotional contours of friendship, love, and departure. Inspired in part by the closing scene of _Wicked_, in which two protagonists reflect on the lasting impact of their bond before parting, the series draws from the artist’s own experience of migration between Puerto Rico and the United States, where distance and displacement shape the rhythms of connection and farewell.

Rendered in luminous nocturnal palettes, Alfredo’s figures—often modeled after himself and closed ones—inhabit surreal landscapes rooted in his hometown of Yabucoa, where mountains, shoreline, and dense vegetation converge beneath expansive night skies. _Te Llevo / I Carry You_ shifts the focus toward what endures beyond it: the people, memories, and emotional inheritances we carry forward. Alfredo charts a tender, introspective journey shaped not only by longing and self-discovery, but by the quiet, transformative power of connection.

Olivera, alongside Colombian-based artist Nicolás Beltrán. This exhibition marks the first occasion on which all five artists present work with the gallery.

In _Still, Moving_, water is not a singular subject but a shifting presence — at once elemental, psychological, architectural, and spiritual. Across distinct practices and perspectives, the exhibition unfolds as body, boundary, memory, and horizon. Water appears suspended, yet never static; contained, yet never fully held.  

For Nicole Burko (b.1987, Toronto, Canada), water is a site of physical and existential encounters. Drawing from her experiences freediving into underwater caverns in a single breath, her immersive oil paintings navigate thresholds between desire and dread, intimacy and mortality. Depth becomes both a literal space and a psychological terrain — a place where stillness heightens awareness and movement becomes survival.

In the work of Ernesto Gutiérrez Moya (b.1995, Havana, Cuba), water emerges through architectural memory. His recurring fountains function as metaphysical anchors — symbols of permanence shaped by impermanence. Formed in the context of growing up in Cuba, these suspended structures hold emotional narratives that feel sensed rather than seen. The fountain, endlessly circulating yet fixed in place, embodies the paradox at the heart of the exhibition: water choreographed, but never entirely controlled.

For Dionnys Matos (b.1991, Holguín, Cuba), the sea embodies duality — nourishment and destruction, promise and rupture. Rooted in the cultural and spiritual presence of Yemayá, the ocean becomes a living force of renewal. Each wave carries both ending and beginning, suggesting that movement itself is a form of continuity.

Meanwhile, Nicolás Beltrán (b. 1992, Ibagué, Colombia) allows water to become the protagonist. Inspired in part by the immersive color fields of Mark Rothko, his monumental shaped-canvas painting pursues dilution and expansion — moments in which perception slows and the visible world opens into contemplation. Rendered at a life-size scale, the work envelops the viewer, allowing motion to quiet into atmosphere.

David E. Olivera (b.1983, Granada, Nicaragua) translates maritime imagery into compositions that oscillate between abstraction and detail. Drawing from subconscious impulse and deliberate observation, his paintings embody collective memory and coastal histories. Movement becomes both physical and emotional — a reflection of freedom, curiosity, and the pull of the horizon.

Together, these works present water as more than scenery or motif. It is a condition of being — fluid, transformative, alive. Whether encountered through the body, architectural memory, spiritual devotion, or abstraction, water becomes a vessel for reflection and connection. In holding motion within the stillness of paint, _Still, Moving_ invites us to consider how transformation is not always visible, and how even the quietest surface carries depth beneath it.

**Spinello Projects presents _Viva La Vida_, a solo exhibition by Venezuelan American artist Bernadette Despujols.**

Through a deeply personal yet universally resonant body of work, Despujols explores the emotional complexities of migration, diaspora, and resilience, showing a glimpse into her lived experiences and those of countless others displaced by political turmoil. In _Viva la Vida_, Bernadette Despujols reflects on the complexities of resilience and joy. Her paintings honor both the vibrancy of endurance and the inevitability of transformation.  This is the artist's second solo exhibition with the gallery.

Rooted in her journey from Venezuela to the United States, Despujols’ paintings address the tensions of leaving one’s homeland, raising children in a foreign country, and navigating the duality of nostalgia and adaptation. Her work embodies both the fragility and strength of the migrant experience, employing heavy, layered brushstrokes that capture the visceral weight of displacement. The body serves as a central motif in her practice, a vessel of memory and transformation, amplifying the role of women and mothers in the diaspora.

Despujols’ visual language is rich with symbols of her homeland, incorporating portraits of Venezuelan immigrants, family members, and friends alongside flowers native to Venezuela, domestic interiors, and animals such as iguanas and dogs. The iguana, recurring throughout her work, takes on multiple meanings—sometimes invasive, sometimes mythical, echoing the dragon motif in her reimagining of Saint Michael as a woman vanquishing a beast. In her painting "Defeated Dragon or Dead Iguana" which portrays her niece holding an iguana carcass, Despujols captures the unsettling juxtaposition of innocence and violence, underscoring the uneasy coexistence of safety and threat within a displaced identity.

For Tremnante's second solo exhibition at the gallery, she continues her series of paintings that depict imagined museum halls, where spectators exist in states of pain, ecstasy, and intrigue. The works are rooted in art history yet deeply responsive to contemporary realities. Tremante’s paintings of museums are, in truth, dreams of museums. The associations between these works and the people who populate her galleries reflect the overlapping realities of pregnancy, violence, and vulnerability—realities that follow women, parents, children, and teenagers across time. In these spaces, figures drift from panic to exuberance, their bodies resisting decorum as they vomit, bleed, weep, conspire, play, read, and dream within settings that traditionally demand silent reverence.

The exhibition features a monumental 14-foot triptych alongside paintings ranging in scale, spanning from 2023 to 2025. Tremante broadens the spectrum of representation in this series, ensuring that the figures in her paintings are not treated as a monolith. Women of varying ages and experiences occupy these spaces—including pregnant figures, a reflection on the increasing restrictions on reproductive rights. The paintings also feature older and disabled women, interrogating the invisibility imposed upon them by society and art history. These figures oscillate between clothed and unclothed states, engaging with art historical contexts that have long dictated the terms of female representation. Her paintings also explore the entanglement of blood and paint in art history, as well as the interchangeability of the two in the narratives of violence and creation that permeate historical imagery.

Tremante’s work is structured around disarming humor and chaos by means of exaggerated objectification, serving as a pointed critique of the ways in which propriety, respectability, and elitism shape our understanding of culture, gender, and motherhood. Tremante invites viewers to examine their own complicity in these narratives while offering an alternative vision of art historical time—one that is weird, and dark—an eternal present and an irreversible succession, sweeping up everything in its path into an uncertain future.

Spinello Projects presents _Of Reverence_, the gallery debut exhibition by LA-based Haitian-American artist Francesca Lalanne (b. 1980, Miami, FL), featuring three different series of engraved steel works, spanning from 2020 to 2024, that investigate the physicality of materials and the immaterial processing of emotions and events. Lelanne engraves on patinated metal, inscribing the immemorial histories of individuals and communities, creating scenes symbolizing the resilience and labor it takes to move through and survive time.

Lalanne depicts several scenes of monumental figures, who with window-like faces carry, crawl, hold, hang, push and pull cryptic weights between structures and across vast backgrounds. The cube, handmade from granite as well as corn and resin, are a recurring symbol in her work that represents both literal and metaphorical weight, is rendered between the hands in her figures or as separate sculptural elements added to the flat plane of the narrative. At times, steel rods emit from the work as anchors into our space, grounding the works in our shared reality. The genderless figures who transcend their individual identity balance and bear these anchors, their gestures, stances, and actions symbolizing burdens, the traumas they move through, and the responsibilities of workers and caregivers. Lalanne’s material investigation involves natural and chemical oxidation processes which produce evolving textures and hues in patina variations, lending a living quality to the metal.

Lalanne is interested in archaic methods of mark-making and recording life, influenced by ancient stone carvings and petroglyphs to 19th century realism. Lalanne draws inspiration from Jean-François Millet’s painting The Gleaners (1857) and Jacques Roumain’s novel Masters of the Dew, honoring the resilience and contributions of farmworkers and essential laborers through her monumental, regal figures. Rooted in the lived experience of the Haitian diaspora and experience as a caseworker, her work shapes secondary trauma into meditative, ritualistic compositions. In her series Lamentations, Lalanne reflects on the collective traumas of 2020, embedding the global grief of the COVID-19 pandemic and the social reckoning after George Floyd’s murder into darker, muted works that bridge personal and shared histories.

Through her explorational use of materials and profound reverence for the interconnectedness of emotions, strength, and survival, Lalanne invites viewers to reflect on the intangible or invisible ways we work and care for each other. Her work serves as a means to recognize the immeasurable value of those whose efforts sustain and enrich our lives.

This exhibition will be featured in the Nova sector of Art Basel Miami Beach, presenting a new series of vessels, mosaic tablets, sculptures, and a ceramic relief mural.

The centerpiece of Greta Chamotta/Great Love is a monumental ceramic wall relief titled Greta Chamotta, meticulously crafted from over 1000 pounds of stoneware ceramic with grog. This kiln-fired mural captures an assemblage of female figures, pagan deities, and gynoids in dynamic movement, drawing from both private and popular memories.

Nina Surel’s use of chamotte, a granular grog obtained from the crushing of clay fired at high temperatures, is prominent in her work. This material infuses her pieces with a sense of danger and resilience, embodying a steadfast presence amidst the ebb and flow of time. Her work pays homage to Afro-Caribbean, Latin, and Mediterranean influences, creating a surrealistic medley of botanical, mythical beings, and bodily forms that reflect a deep connection with the environment and the mysteries of nature.

In addition to the mural, Greta Chamotta/Great Love features a collection of ceramic tablets, sculptures, and vessels. Her hand-built coiled vessels and mosaic reliefs chronicle the myriad experiences of womanhood, from the joys of childbirth to the pains of loss, emphasizing the resilient interconnectedness of nature and our bodies. Surel’s works, which include motifs such as ovaries, native Florida beauty berries, and cells, explore themes of slow sexuality, transformation, and the beauty of imperfection. The Attalea Palm tree seed, exaggerated into shapes resembling breasts, serves as a potent symbol of fertility and transformation in Surel’s narrative. Just as the conch shell amplifies sound, Surel’s art amplifies the voices and stories of women, connecting them across time and space through her intricate and deeply symbolic visual language. The female figures in Nina Surel’s work are often fragmented and remixed with body parts seamlessly combined with plants and animals, symbolizing their interconnectedness and representing alter egos, mothers and daughters, sisters, or different versions of the same person through time.

Surel’s use of collage creates a visual tapestry that blends historical, mythological, and natural elements. She is inspired from a wide range of sources, including the supreme goddess Atabey of the Taínos, the caracara bird, and native plants. Surel finds the symbolic connection between Gradiva, “the \[Pompeiian\] woman who walks,” and Gravida, the state of pregnancy, to delve into themes of creation, journey, and the evolution of the female form. Within the hard matter of grog and earth, shells whisper stories of resilience and transformation, akin to the German name “Greta,” echoing pearls hidden in the depths. “Chamotta," like a tough cookie, embodies strength and beauty, melding earthen material with symbolism, a testament to enduring nature.

Her works serve as a testament to the enduring power of myths and the indomitable spirit of women. Nina Surel’s visual vocabulary is deeply personal and evocative, inviting viewers to contemplate the intricate narratives of identity, memory, and the feminine experience.

Spinello Projects presents _Dream Animal_, the US debut exhibition of Damien Cifelli. In this exhibition, Cifelli continues his exploration of the world of Tarogramma, the artist’s imagined society that mirrors our own yet diverges in fundamental ways. Through a suite of paintings and drawings, _Dream Animal_ invites viewers into a parallel universe where its inhabitants search for meaning and chase discovery.

Tarogramma is a world of Cifelli’s construction, where the norms and structures in our world are irrelevant. As such, dwellers of this place exist on their own; while plants are pervasive, animals are nonexistent. In one painting, a group of researchers gaze at an unknown biological specimen. Could this be the origin of life in their world or are plants the catalyst to answers? Central to _Dream Animal_ is the fictive documentation of researchers and searchers within Tarogramma—citizens who are engaged in a search for understanding, both of their world and themselves. These figures in Cifelli’s paintings are individuals with lives, dreams, and purpose. These people are sometimes collectively identified by gold pins and pearl armbands, and undertake various forms of research, from examining unknown organisms to exploring the desolate world of Tarogramma, in both transcendental and analytical realms. Their work reflects the broader existential questions that permeate Tarogramma, as both the inhabitants and the viewer grapple with the nature of consciousness and the limits of their understanding. In _Dream Animal_, the viewer is an explorer, documenting and deciphering the world of Tarogramma, much like an anthropologist or ethnographer would study an unfamiliar culture.

The characters, environments, and objects within Tarogramma may appear recognizable at first glance, but they operate under an entirely different cultural code. In Tarogramma, symbols are imbued with disassociated meanings unrelated to what we think they could be. Iconography, such as flags or emblems represent regions that exist not as physical places but as ideas or states of mind. Tarogramma is a society without ethnic, cultural, and gender hierarchy. In this world, identity is fluid and chosen rather than externally assigned, allowing for constant transformation and reinvention. 

The creation of Tarogramma is an ongoing process of simultaneous discovery and invention, where each new work adds to the whole and gains meaning about the larger world Cifelli has built. The exhibition presents these works as part of a broader narrative, where the boundaries of time and space are fluid, and the viewer becomes both a visitor and an interpreter. _Dream Animal_ is a reminder that there are infinite, unimaginable tools for making renewed sense of the world. Cifelli invites us to abandon conventions and embrace the uncertainty and endless possibilities of this strange and compelling world.

Spinello Projects presents _I’m Gonna Getcha_, a two person show by Alejandra Moros and Thomas Bils. This exhibition offers an intimate look into the creative dialogue between these close friends and colleagues, whose artistic practices have influenced each other in profound and unexpected ways.

The impetus for this exhibition emerged from a painting trade between the artists, where both depicted a close-up of an anole, a lizard with both native and invasive subspecies in Florida, hanging from an earlobe in a piece titled _I’m Gonna Getcha_. This shared creative act initiates a broader aesthetic and thematic conversation that unfolds playfully throughout the exhibition à la exquisite corpse. The works of Moros and Bils, while distinct in style and approach, engage in a chummy visual dialogue that reflects their deep personal and artistic connection.

Known for her meticulous ability to imbue her images with a supernatural glow, Moros steps into the world of her paintings with a renewed sense of exploration. Using images sourced from public and personal photo archives, Moros’ works map her evolving interests in adaptation, evolution, and metamorphosis. Her paintings, marked by luminescent hues, intuitive cropping, and exaggerated elements, offer an analysis of the body as a tool and the subtleties of time summoning transformation.

Thomas Bils complements Moros’ by capturing mundane yet perplexing scenes. Bils’ works offer intrigue with a continuing visual inquiry into the nature of perception, reality, and the role of the artist as a world builder and jester. His paintings build images that invite deeper noticing, focusing on the tension between what is known, mysterious, safe dangerous, and normal or abnormal.

Both artists explore liminal spaces, though in different contexts. For Moros, the liminal space exists in the macro, where the body becomes a landscape, and the boundaries between shape and meaning blur. Bils’ primarily paints liminal moments in time. Each painting is a snapshot of a point of view where life is cryptic and something is about to happen. They engage deeply with the concept of defamiliarization and stasis. Alejandra Moros’ paintings transform familiar body parts and everyday objects into something alien and indeterminate through extreme close-ups and hyper detail, capturing the intimate and vast, a sensation that can be as disorienting as it is familiar. Bils’ painting, on the other hand, is parafictional diary where objects and scenes toe the line between being staged and candid. He plays on the narratorial quality of objects when placed in proximity; things are off–close to a paradox but not quite opposites. Bils, too, works with stasis, particularly in how painting as a medium can capture a moment in an action, freezing its absurdity, and then itself, becoming an artifact. These implicit concepts lead them to use proxy scenes for life and death. In Bils’ paintings life and death swim together, while Moros’ paintings are about life, but life in the way that death comes before it, offering room for new growth.

One of the exhibition’s highlights is a suite of paintings of Bils' beloved cat, Egg, rendered by both artists. This space encapsulates their creative exchange, offering viewers a glimpse into the fun that defines their relationship. Whether through the shared subject of Egg or the thematic parallels in their broader work, _I’m Gonna Getcha_ showcases the rich playfulness of ideas, techniques, and sensations that these two artists bring to the discourse of painting.

Alfredo, a rising voice in contemporary painting, continues to build upon his exploration of identity, queerness, and cinematic storytelling. In this new body of work, Alfredo transports viewers to vividly rendered terrains—ranging from the alien-like mountains of Iceland to the dream-like deserts of Utah and Arizona, and the tree-covered peaks of Puerto Rico. These landscapes, inspired by his travels, serve as backdrops for the unfolding of intricate, multi-layered saga.

Alfredo introduces new characters into his visual lexicon while still using his own figure as a central motif. His paintings oscillate between the literal and the dreamlike, inviting interpretations that blur the lines between reality and fantasy. Drawing direct inspiration from iconic films such as Titanic, The Wizard of Oz, The Sound of Music, and La La Land, Alfredo’s work serves as a homage to cinematic history, while also recontextualizing these references within his unique world.

Alfredo captures moments reminiscent of young couples sneaking out at night, embarking on forbidden adventures that lead to profound self-discovery. These nocturnal journeys unfold in liminal spaces where the boundaries between reality and dream blur, echoing the characters’—and Alfredo’s own—confrontations with their inner truths. This subtly pushes back against the resistance to queerness in mainstream culture, using the language of cinematic history to carve out space for queer identities within the visual canon now reimagined through the medium of painting.

In Alfredo’s world, his characters navigate landscapes that are both monumental and intimate, where emotions like curiosity, wonder, concern, and admiration guide them through their complex inner lives. These emotions are woven into the landscapes themselves, with recurring motifs like a distant green laser or a red glow creating visual connections across the series, reinforcing the narrative unity of his imagined universe. The dominant use of blue evokes the depth and stillness of night, echoing the exaggerated blue tones often seen in cinematic nighttime scenes. Esaí Alfredo’s presentation at The Armory Show invites viewers into a world that is both familiar and strange, a place where the echoes of pop culture and the artist’s personal history collide to create something entirely new. This body of work continues to solidify Alfredo’s reputation as a painter whose ability to merge the personal with the universal offers a compelling lens through which to view contemporary identity and experience.

Jaffe began her professional career studying archeology and anthropology, examining how people create and express meaning and values through objects, rituals, and behaviors This exhibition continues this exploration by presenting bronze, wood, resin, clay and cast paper sculptures from her Pre-Verbal Series. Body fragments, vegetative processes, and microscopic life fuse, mutate, and morph, and the resulting objects invite recognition, while remaining mutable, suggestive, and indeterminate., inviting viewers to navigate the complexities of meaning-making and memory. Accompanying the sculptures are drawings incorporating calligraphic prints and objects made of cotton linters. These drawings continue the dialogue proposed in the sculptures further exploring the mutable nature of form and memory.  Also included in this exhibition is a stop motion animation “Alice in Dystopia” a contemporary restructuring and retelling of Alice in Wonderland which is an example of her work that reexamines cultural stories.

Much of Jaffe’s work creates a language that explores the realms of the unconscious and dream states, all aspects of experience where meaning is created through metaphor, multiple associations, memory, and collective storytelling. Her work has a connection to surrealism, where the world and its forms are familiar yet strange and a bit unsettling.

Exploring how we form identity, from the earliest pre-verbal stages of their life through the introduction into language and cultural conditioning  motivates Jaffe to create artworks that reconnect people with their own interior experiences and to create agency and new alternatives of being in contemporary culture.

This was a period of social stigmatization associated with homosexuality and AIDS, with an overarching “don’t ask don’t tell” approach to LGBTQ+ issues and culture. Almost 30 years later in the midst of his painting career, he is still influenced by would-be mentors and photographers whose lives and careers were cut short by AIDS, such as, Robert Mapplethorpe, Stanley Stellar, Mark Morrisroe, and Peter Hujar, among others. The paintings in Forever Endeavor And Ever reference notable photographs that chronicled gay life and culture in the late 70’s and 80’s and act as odes to a specific generation of artists. The works simultaneously employ narrative-driven iconography culled from mythology, religion, art history, and folklore as well as current issues like climate change and migration to create ambiguous scenes that feel strangely familiar.

The figure in Atlas crossing the Darién Gap is depicted on crutches hobbling down a steep mountain slope against a red forest. His overburdened rucksack and thick plaster leg cast render him pathetic. Upon closer inspection his beleaguered gaze suggests that perhaps he is a migrant carrying his whole world on his back. The trio in Trinity River form a triangulated neo-classical composition unfolding as a waterside retreat, but the toxic colored landscape, discrepancy in attire, and vacant stares suggest that they have each endured their own personal baptism by fire.

The suite of seven portraits on mylar included in the exhibition are a mixture of drawing and painting rendered on both sides of translucent drafting film that also rely on cross-cultural references. Linus (After Stellar) is modeled after an erotic photograph by Stanley Stellar conceptually overlaid with an allusion to the existentially anxious blanket toting Peanuts character Linus. The Contortionist (After Hujar) mixes its homage to Peter Hujar’s photos of Daniel Schook with Magritte’s Ceci N’est Pas Une Pipe. The streaming rays that land on the boy’s head in The Ecstasy of St. Bernini are borrowed from the baroque sculpture of Saint. Teresa With a clasped head, the figure’s posture suggests more shame, guilt and torment than the ecstasy depicted in Bernini’s original work and hints at recent scandals laid bare within the church.

Visual oxymorons drive this new body of work. The paintings are colorful and vibrant, but dark and dense. They are simultaneously humorous yet poignant, beautiful but off-putting. The characters confront the viewer with jaded glassy eyed stares that thinly veil deeper intimacies. Although many works in the exhibition point to doom, despair, and melancholy, they also celebrate and revel in it. There is absurdity and romance to all of these predicaments. The cast of characters inhabiting the works have taken lessons from the past and their predecessors. They are well versed on the myriad contradictions that lay ahead. Alone in their solitude, they “Party Like It’s 1999”.

Spinello Projects is proud to present _Superhost_ by Canadian artist, Kris Knight, debuting a series of figurative paintings inspired by the historical notion of urban exodus during an epidemic. _Superhost_ is Knight’s pandemic garden series, inspired by the similarities of Victorian wellness during the tuberculosis pandemic of the 18th and 19th centuries and the connective social patterns to that of COVID19. These paintings return to the idea of being alone in the sense of wholeness: alone as in “all one.” Knight’s characters retreat from the muchness of their urban worlds for the stillness of gardens, country homes and rural Airbnbs. He cites his contemporary characters in bucolic locations referencing historical Victorian and Belle Époque garden paintings and expands his pastel palette to include the vivid, acidic greens that were popular during this era.

However, much like his prior works, a sense of quiet desire gives way to despair: the foliage of the garden becomes encroaching, window muntins feel like prison bars, and cabin fever sets in. Knight’s character’s indifference inevitably falters when reality creeps in that no one is immune to loss, sickness, or heartbreak. Nostalgia intensifies when restrictions arise and the desire to escape is insatiable. Like the shifting moods of his characters, the comforting green of a garden drenched in jubilance eventually fades to the cool moonlit shadows. Like many queer urbanites with rural backgrounds who felt alienated growing up, Knight’s complicated relationship with the country is evident in these works. The desire for belonging, mixed with never feeling at ease or safe, carries into adulthood and subtly plagues tender portraits and bucolic scenes of this exhibition.

A pandemic shakes the stupor out of life and dramatizes the truth of our condition: we are all vulnerable and cannot escape our common humanity and fate. Superhost invites the viewer into the private moments of his characters, demonstrating the conflict between aloneness and oneness.

Using a range of weaving and embellishing techniques such as hand weaving on a four shaft loom, industrial photo weaving machine looms, and hand stitched appliques, Arango Palacios creates seductive images of men, blending the masculine figure with soft eroticism and feminine qualities.

The male body is featured prominently in this body of work. The depiction of nude or partially nude male bodies are not only a nod to the history of eroticism in queer art, but also a reference to hook-up app culture. Online hook-up apps like Grindr and Sniffies are filled with images of people who often exclude their face to maintain discretion, but simultaneously flaunt their bodies to express their sexuality. While their identity is not disclosed, there are other clues into these people’s personalities or identities. Tattoos, body hair, jewelry, and clothing (or the lack thereof) are not only an individual’s idiosyncrasy but they are also a key to attracting the male gaze, stimulating further connections.

By placing the figures in a ‘jardín’ or garden background, Arango Palacios is bringing these found online images into a fantastical setting that posits safety, security, and freedom as a given, in contrast to an actual society that is plagued by machismo, homophobia, transphobia, xenophobia, and urbanization. Instead of speaking on the violence, shame and guilt caused by these phobias and conditions, these textile works celebrate the beauty and love that resides in queer bodies.

It is this feeling that Celin gracefully hones in on his paintings either overtly through images of lovers and friends or through the smallest details that fill in the stories of these paintings. The process of remembering is intertwined with Celin’s process, as he draws from his own experiences as a gay immigrant to create this body of work.

Celin’s paintings depict languid, fluid, and beautiful people, who can’t help but seem distant and longing. These subjects share space, their bodies, and sensations of postcolonial restlessness. They seek to belong, finding each other in the dance clubs, and bedrooms that populate cities. As curator and writer, Paul Clinton, puts it, “unstable attachments \[relationships\] might be the core of Celin’s project \[exhibition\], offering a model of belonging that is neither essentializing nor conforms to the universalizing call for queers to be citizens of nowhere, a position the sexile \[sex-exiles\] can hardly afford.”

At the heart of _Florida Beauty_ lies a monumental stoneware ceramic bas-relief mural, kiln-fired to 2160°F for over 20 hours. In this mural, 3000 pounds of heavy grog stoneware ceramic convey the thriving spirit of the people who have settled and flourished in Florida, reflecting the enduring community that emerges from artistic expression. This artwork is a testament to the richness of Florida, featuring forms and living organisms native to the state, such as Coontie, Florida Beauty berry, Seagrape, and Cocoplum. Fostering relations of solidarity and interdependence among diverse beings, it symbolically connects the dots between human, animal, myth, the organic and cyborg, bridging historical, ecological, and anatomical dimensions.

Surel uses collage to sketch out the imagery in her mural and ceramic tablets and vases. Her use of collage as a creative method helps her structure her visuals. Sgraffito is the technique she uses in her tables and vases of scratching through a colored glaze to reveal the clay body beneath. The sgraffito technique employed in the tablets and vessels adds a layer of storytelling, chronicling women's experiences, including sex, abortion, pregnancy, and childbirth. Made with the same intention, Surel's Core Vessel series is an immersive installation that celebrates the female body as a vessel. Each vessel, cast from anonymous women's pelvises, houses a rare Florida Beauty Philodendron. These sculptures embody the strength and resilience of the human body and the possibility of reinvention. The installation is flanked by two-dimensional terracotta on canvas abstractions which were created in the process of casting the vessels.

Nina Surel's art explores life's rituals, drawing from art history and her personal journey. She captures transformation, aging, resilience, and fragility in mediums like clay, plants, and raw canvas. _Florida Beauty_ narrates a journey through time, blending past, present, and future. Within Surel's work lies an esoteric realm, where nature morphs into magic, belief trumps knowledge, and ritual transcends reason. Circular time challenges conventional history.

Inspired by the "cyborg manifesto," Surel's art envisions a world beyond stereotypes, exploring identity, transformation, and our profound connection to the Earth. The exhibition echoes Donna Haraway's "staying with the trouble," celebrating women's role in nurturing a sustainable world and embracing a diverse, non-binary reality. It reconnects with matriarchal legacies, honoring the timeless, feminine earth.

This work conceptually intersects the use of mark making with the imperceptibility of living systems while imagining a blooming landscape of flowers in the night.

She became interested in ways labor is invisible but its product is obvious to the point of being taken for granted, and has transferred that theory towards the use of the line in drawing as it relates how the trajectory of the line manifests her body's movements and her emotional control. She became obsessed with getting from point A to point B and still experiences this obsession in the process of making her work. Over time she has worked towards understanding the specificity of creating a line and the specificity of her mark making.

With the drawings presented in this show Alfonso works with color as opposed to previous forays using only black or white. Initially taking inspiration from her time in nature and studying the destruction of native prairie lands in Texas, she is influenced by the invisible structures that uphold life within the living system of flowers which interact with the entirety of the ecological landscape and which sustains life for all beings. This drawing in particular comes out of Alfonso’s recent experiences biking long distances in the Florida Everglades. While using these ideas as the framework for her newest drawings, she takes her body to the extreme with this 108 foot long drawing creating a color gradient in soft pastels as the ground for layers of abstract, unencumbered scrawling lines, reminiscent of Monet’s Water Lilies (1897-1926) and Joan Mitchell’s color fields (1950’s - 1992). Spinello Projects presents Back to Basics, the Miami gallery debut of Alexandre Diop (b. 1995), a Franco-Senegalese artist currently based in Vienna, Austria, featuring new works that uniquely combine abstraction and figuration. For this exhibition, Diop is revisiting the birthplace of his artistic practice, the city of Berlin, to be the inspirational center. Diop’s works bridge painting and sculpture and occupy a space that allows him to experiment with definitions of object versus image. Diop builds artworks from materials commonly found in his everyday surroundings – metal, wood, textile, latex, animal fibers, burnt materials, leather, rope, plaster, old car parts, rust, books, photographs, etc. Materiality is a technical expression of his investigations that also interpret music, film, and literary influences. His spontaneous process focuses on composition and decomposition, revealing answers about the entanglement of art, and life, and bringing to the fore notions of existence and conscious observation; he considers the basics of human interaction and his own artistic trajectory. Diop presents himself as an observer of history and contemporary society - a citizen of the world who acknowledges the realities surrounding him.

Back to Basics will run concurrently with the artist’s solo presentation at the Rubell Museum, debuting new works created at the museum’s 2022 Artist-in-Residence.

[**NIGHTFALL**](https://spinelloprojects.com/program/#nightfall)

11\. 28 – 01\. 14. 2023

- [Esaí Alfredo](https://spinelloprojects.com/artist/esai-alfredo/)

Spinello Projects presents NIGHTFALL, the Miami gallery debut of Esaí Alfredo (b. 1997). Alfredo explores the themes of gay love, light pollution, curiosity and faith in the natural world, and human disconnection from it in his painting series, NIGHTFALL. NIGHTFALL is a series of oil paintings based on a 1941 science fiction short story of the same title by Issac Asimov. Alfredo, inspired by disaster cinema, recontextualizes the story to take place in the present era on a Caribbean island and centers around young lovers, who grow closer as they investigate the science behind a weeklong eclipse that terrifies the superstitious population around them. Alfredo also serves his own image as a model in these paintings and works with radical contrasting colors to bring to life the surreal quality of light in the atmosphere of his works. This is the artist’s first US solo exhibition.

[**I Came to See the Damage That Was Done and the Treasures That Prevail**](https://spinelloprojects.com/program/#i-came-to-see-the-damage-that-was-done-and-the-treasures-that-prevail)

09\. 24 – 10\. 29. 2022

- [Antonia Wright](https://spinelloprojects.com/artist/antonia-wright/)

Spinello Projects presents I Came to See the Damage That Was Done and the Treasures That Prevail, a breath of work Wright created over the last several years as a fierce reaction to the women’s reproductive rights crisis embodied in resistance and beauty, vulnerability and power.

As an artist, mother, and board member of Planned Parenthood, Wright presents her newest digital artwork installation, Women in Labor, a generative sound art composition that uses data sonification to protest the changing laws around access to safe and legal abortion. Through computational algorithms, the piece sonifies the increase in mileage a woman will now have to travel to access care. Partnering with midwives, the artist has been collecting the sounds women make during labor starting with her own home birth experience in 2015.

The exhibition’s title is a line taken from Adrienne Rich’s poem Diving into the Wreck which also includes performative videos using Wright’s pregnant body, large format cyanotypes made with the figure and light, and sculpture.

[**Blood and Bodies, Mingled and Imperfect**](https://spinelloprojects.com/program/#blood-and-bodies-mingled-and-imperfect)

09\. 24 – 10\. 29. 2022

- Elizabeth Tremante

Spinello Projects is proud to present Blood and Bodies, Mingled and Imperfect, a solo exhibition of recent works by Elizabeth Tremante. Imagine art history as a series of artworks arranged along a linear piece of yarn stretched straight and flat. Now roll that yarn into a ball and imagine all the points of contact, interference, and meaning that arise.

The narrative structure of Elizabeth Tremante’s paintings is simple: people in museums and galleries looking at art. The art has been curated to accidentally reveal a poignant or darkly comic psychological undercurrent that is sensed and felt before it is understood. The museum-goers in the paintings exclusively include women, parents, caregivers, and children experiencing varying levels of dissociation, panic, and stress. Their bodies act out, are out of control, distorted, or are beginning to merge with the artworks and exhibition spaces themselves.

Her work creates absurd and comic scenarios that touch upon issues in people’s lives, such as the precarious intertwining of motherhood, parenthood, and artisthood. It meditates on endless art historical representations of the feminine to glorify and control women, girls, and their bodies, presently and historically. The “curated exhibitions” depicted in her paintings are her versions of existing artworks, mostly from Western art history. Pulled together in ahistorical groupings, the exhibitions find new meaning in how the works relate to each other. This exposes painful blindspots in art history that mirror the sexism, subtle power dynamics, and bias in contemporary culture. The figures, artworks, fashion choices, and spaces are painted in various levels of detail, description, and sophistication of color relationships in order to create visual hierarchies that tell the story just as well. The artworks depicted inside the paintings have been altered from the “originals,” showing distorted faces, blood gushing from the artwork into the galleries, decapitated sculptures, and scale changes. In these works, female subjects that were sexualized in the original are newly recreated with even more brazen and exaggerated objectification. These paintings use awkward comedy to takedown ideas about propriety, respect, and elitism; they invite people to examine their own culpability or teach us to interrogate unchallenged or received knowledge about culture, gender, and motherhood.

[**Entre Dos Mundos**](https://spinelloprojects.com/program/#entre-dos-mundos)

04\. 16 – 06\. 04. 2022

- Elliot & Erick Jiménez

Elliot & Erick Jiménez’s debut solo exhibition, _Entre Dos Mundos_, which translates to “_Between Two Worlds_”, visualizes through staged photographs the personification of deities and saints within Yoruba and Catholic syncretism, or Lucumí. Lucumí, also known as Santeria, meaning “way of the saints”, is a concept enmeshed in the culture and spiritual life of many Cubans and Cuban Americans.

Raised in a Cuban biracial family, Elliot & Erick were exposed to a variety of religious practices in Catholicism and Santeria, or Lucumí, on both sides of their family which illuminated them to the parallels and divergent tangents of the two spiritual worlds.

Enslaved Yorubans of West Africa developed Lucumí in Cuba to continue practicing their traditional religion Isese, under the guise of worship of Catholic saints throughout Spanish colonial domination. Catholic saints became placeholders for Yoruban orishas, or deities, who themselves are icons for themes in the natural world, represented by colors. Lucumí went from a hidden, closed practice to an accepted part of culture in Cuban society that exists side by side with Catholicism and Christianity, despite the anti-clericalism of Cuban politics. Even though there is a population wide understanding and general tolerance of Lucumí in Cuban society, Catholicism is still used to mask Lucumí or Santero practices by some, as obscurity, mysticism, and at times, stigma, overshadow the religion.

Through images reminiscent of Cuban artist Belkis Ayón’s work, Elliot & Erick translate obscurity and mysticism as functions of power using elusive anonymous figures, facelessness, and symbols to reinterpret and imagine the orishas through a contemporary pictorial lens. The feminine figure, the queer, ambiguous, and alluring are intertwined and brought into proximity to the power dynamics of the orishas and their Catholic sibling saints and God. Elliot & Erick represent themselves, twin brothers, as Ibejí, the venerated twin orishas, further expressing their lived experience within the practice of Lucumí. Still life photographs of flowers complement images of the orishas. Flowers hold significance in Lucumí as offerings loaded with emotional power. Although still lives, the flower images contain visible movement which is created in camera through multiple exposures and experimentation with light, therefore subjecting something as innocuous as flowers, to possess a caliginous and dynamic ethereal energy.Elliot & Erick are influenced by western esotericism and its manifestations in literature and cinema, and gothic, baroque, and renaissance aesthetics within contemporary visual culture. The natural world, identity, duality and cultural heritage are the grounds for this exhibition and underlies the transculturation they experience as Cuban-American artists.

[**Talking to Real Americans**](https://spinelloprojects.com/program/#talking-to-real-americans)

01\. 29 – 03\. 05. 2022

- [Eddie Arroyo](https://spinelloprojects.com/artist/eddie-arroyo/)

Spinello Projects presents _Talking to Real Americans_, a gallery-wide solo exhibition by Eddie Arroyo. This exhibition is a continuation of Arroyo’s documentation of scenes and subjects in flux within the day-to-day reality of living in an American capitalist hegemony. The scenes and subjects in these paintings depict people contending against imposed power and places nascent with this power. In this presentation, several bodies of work exist. Some portray specific actions and interactions that Arroyo himself has been involved in or witnessed with members of different communities and grassroots organizations around the country. End Title 42, Black Lives Matter, and FTP are some of the actions represented in these works. Some paintings record buildings and places fraught with deterioration and speculative change, Chinatown, Little Haiti, Allapattah, and the Everglades, for example. 

One can start to understand why Arroyo paints reading his statement below:

_Let us walk. It has occurred to me that we have been practicing the exercise of assimilation. We come to this country, or in my case, born into it, but never really fit in. Despite my best efforts, there will never be that feeling of being absolutely home. And so here we are talking about what it means to be a grateful immigrant, a worthy citizen, and of course a Real American. It seems like the guidelines shift but there are consistencies, one being the absolute acknowledgment of law and order._ 

_Following the guidelines of the state is fundamental; it is the first signifier of a Real American, who enjoys a higher degree of self-determination. To be a worthy citizen requires the right language to speak properly and communicate concerns. Of course, there is a visual component, one that is acceptable to the state. Now, this comes in various forms, not simply driven by how one dresses or carries oneself, but initially how one looks. This is racial. There is and continues to be an abundance of evidence to reinforce this bias. Through assimilation one may mitigate tension within the state, contemplating, as “real Americans” and worthy citizens, what to do with the grateful immigrant? The nature of which is to absolutely integrate our society by the standards of the state. It is a familiar process and will continue to inform us what it means to live in this country._ 

Talking to Real Americans is on view at the Gesamtkunstwerk Building located at 2930 NW 7th Avenue from January 29th, 2022 till March 5th, 2022. Schedule your appointment at info(at)spinelloprojects.com. Free and open to the public.
